note: Demo values, not secret. Educational code, not constant-time.

sections.title: What goes wrong if k is reused

glossary.private key: The secret number d. Whoever knows it can sign in the owner's name.
glossary.public key: The point Q = d · G. Everyone may know it; it is used to check signatures.
glossary.point: A pair of numbers (x, y) that satisfies the curve equation. Points can be added to each other, and adding a point to itself k times is written k · G.
glossary.base point: A fixed starting point G that everyone agrees on. Every key is a multiple of it.
glossary.mod n: Arithmetic that wraps around at n, like a clock wraps around at 12. For example 10 + 5 mod 12 = 3.
glossary.share: One piece of a secret. Each piece alone looks random; only all pieces together give the secret.
glossary.hash: A fingerprint of a message: a fixed-size number that changes completely if the message changes.
glossary.nonce: A number used once. In ECDSA it must be random, secret and new for every signature.
glossary.inverse: The number that undoes a multiplication: k⁻¹ · k = 1 mod n. It plays the role of division.
glossary.x coordinate: The first of the two numbers that make up a point.
glossary.signature: The pair (r, s). It proves that the message was signed with the private key that belongs to Q.
glossary.low s: s and n − s both pass the check. Using only the smaller one makes every signature unique.

steps.title: Choose the private key
steps.description: The private key d is a random number between 1 and n - 1. Whoever knows d can sign.
steps.plain: Think of d as a password that is never shown to anyone. Because it is picked at random from a huge range, nobody can guess it.

steps.title: Compute the public key
steps.description: Q is d copies of the base point G added together. Going from d to Q is easy, going back from Q to d is the hard problem that keeps the key safe.
steps.plain: Q is like a padlock made from the password. Everyone may see the padlock and use it to check signatures, but nobody can work out the password from it.

steps.title: Pick the first share
steps.description: Instead of one device holding d, it is split into two parts. The first part d₁ is a random number. It goes to Alice.
steps.plain: Instead of one device holding the whole password, we tear it into two pieces. Alice gets the first piece, a plain random number.

steps.title: Compute the second share
steps.description: The second part is whatever is missing to reach d. It goes to Bob. Since d₁ is random, d₂ on its own also looks random.
steps.plain: Bob gets exactly the piece that is missing. On its own, either piece is just a random number and says nothing about d.

steps.title: The shares add up to d
steps.description: Only both parts together give back the key. Each part alone fits every possible d.
steps.plain: Only both pieces together give back the password. In the two-party protocol this never actually happens: Alice and Bob will sign without putting the pieces together.

steps.title: Public parts of the shares
steps.description: Each device can publish d₁ · G or d₂ · G. They add up to the public key Q, without anyone learning d.
steps.plain: Each piece has its own padlock, and the two padlocks combine into the same public key Q as before. To the outside world nothing has changed.
steps.formula: Q₁ = d₁ · G,  Q₂ = d₂ · G,  Q = Q₁ + Q₂

steps.title: Hash the message
steps.description: Signing works on a number, not on text. The message is hashed with SHA-256 and the result is reduced mod n.
steps.plain: The message is turned into a fingerprint number. Changing even one letter gives a completely different number.

steps.title: Choose a nonce
steps.description: k is a fresh random number for every signature. It must stay secret and must never be used twice (see the last section).
steps.plain: A one-time random number, used for this signature only, like a fresh seal for every letter.

steps.title: Compute the nonce point
steps.description: Same operation as for the public key, now with k.
steps.plain: The one-time number gets its own point, the same way the password got its padlock Q.

steps.title: Take its x coordinate
steps.description: The first half of the signature is the x coordinate of R, reduced mod n.
steps.plain: Only one coordinate of that point is kept. It becomes the first half of the signature.

steps.title: Invert the nonce
steps.description: k⁻¹ is the number that gives 1 when multiplied with k mod n.
steps.plain: In this number system there is no ordinary division. Instead we multiply by the inverse, the number that undoes multiplying by k.

steps.title: Compute s
steps.description: The second half of the signature mixes the hash, r and the private key.
steps.plain: This line ties the message, the password and the one-time number together. Only someone who knows d can produce an s that fits.
steps.formula: s = k⁻¹ · (e + r · d) mod n

steps.title: Use the low form of s
steps.description: Both s and n − s verify. Bitcoin and libsecp256k1 accept only the smaller one, so if s is above n / 2 it is replaced by n − s.
steps.plain: Every signature has a twin that also passes the check. To make signatures unique, the smaller twin is always used.
steps.formula: if s > n / 2:  s = n − s

steps.title: Invert s
steps.description: The verifier knows Q, the message and (r, s), but not d or k.
steps.plain: Now someone else checks the signature. They only use public things: the message, the signature and the public key.

steps.title: First factor
steps.plain: The first of two helper numbers, made from the message fingerprint.

steps.title: Second factor
steps.plain: The second helper number, made from the first half of the signature.

steps.title: Rebuild the nonce point
steps.description: If the signature is honest, u₁ · G + u₂ · Q is the same point R the signer used, because u₁ + u₂ · d = k mod n.
steps.plain: With the helpers and the padlock Q, the checker rebuilds a point. If the signature is honest, it is the same point R the signer made, although the checker never saw k or d.

steps.title: Compare with r
steps.description: The signature is valid if the x coordinate of P matches r.
steps.plain: If the rebuilt point matches the first half of the signature, the signature is genuine.

steps.title: Multiplicative to additive conversion
steps.description: Alice holds a, Bob holds b. MtA turns the product a · b into two shares alpha + beta = a · b mod n without either side learning the other's input. Planned: we are waiting for the description from our supervisors.
steps.plain: A way for two people to multiply their secret numbers without showing them to each other. Each one ends up with a piece of the result.

steps.title: Joint signature
steps.description: Alice and Bob create k together and use MtA for the products of secrets, so they produce a normal (r, s) without ever putting d together. Planned: follows once MtA is in place.
steps.plain: Alice and Bob produce one normal signature together. Nobody can tell from the signature that two devices were involved.

steps.title: Sign a second message with the same k
steps.description: A buggy signer uses k again for another message. Both signatures have the same r, so anyone can see that k was reused.
steps.plain: The signer makes a mistake: the same one-time number is used for a second message.
steps.formula: s₂ = k⁻¹ · (e₂ + r · d) mod n

steps.title: Recover the nonce
steps.description: Subtracting the two equations for s removes d. Because of the low-s rule the attacker does not know if s or s₂ was flipped, so they try s − s₂ and s + s₂ with both signs and keep the guess that leads to Q.
steps.plain: Two signatures with the same one-time number give two equations with the same unknowns. Like a school algebra problem, the attacker can solve them.

steps.title: Recover the private key
steps.description: With k known, the equation for s has only one unknown left: d.
steps.plain: Once k is known, the password follows directly from the formula for s.
steps.formula: d = (s · k − e) · r⁻¹ mod n

steps.title: Check against the public key
steps.description: The recovered d gives the public key Q. The key is lost.
steps.plain: The attacker checks the result against the public padlock. It fits: they can now sign anything in the owner's name.
